title: Rama's hard words
hookLine: the reunion everyone has waited for, and the hardest words in the epic
carry: raja dharma, and the freedom to question it

cards: For months, everything in this story has pointed to one moment. The search parties, the leap, the ring, the jewel, the bridge, the war.

Now Vibhishana brings Sita out of the grove, bathed and dressed in fine clothes, carried toward Rama through a crowd of monkeys and rakshasas pressing to see her. Rama says: let her walk, so everyone can see.
She steps down and walks toward him, shy and full of joy, looking at his face. What happens next has troubled readers, inside the tradition and out.

teach.b: Rama does not take her in his arms. In Valmiki he speaks coldly, in front of everyone. I've won you back, he says, and wiped out the insult to my family's name.
But know this: I didn't fight this war for you.

teach.h: NOT FOR YOU, BUT FOR MY HONOR.
teach.b: I fought it for my honor. Then come the words that hurt most. She lived in another man's house for a long time, and he doesn't feel he can take her back.
She's free to go wherever she likes. Valmiki doesn't soften it.
Sita weeps, ashamed in front of the crowd, and those watching are shaken too. Hindus call Rama maryada purushottam, the best of men, who keeps every bound of duty. So how can he speak like this?
Many teachers read the scene through raja dharma, a king's duty: a king must be seen to be beyond suspicion, so Rama speaks as a king, not a husband, putting his people's trust above his own heart.
Some read it as a test meant for the world, not for Sita.
Other readers, Hindu and not, find it simply wrong and side with Sita, and women's songs and regional Ramayanas give her side at length.

teach.h: DHARMA IS SUBTLE. YOU MAY ASK.
teach.b: Here's the teaching under all of it: dharma is subtle, and Hinduism doesn't ask you to stop thinking when you open its holiest stories. The tradition argues about dharma out loud, even Rama's. Tomorrow, Sita answers.

how: Hindu teachers, scholars and storytellers discuss this scene from many sides, and some retellings, including women's songs and regional Ramayanas, give Sita's side of it at length.

games.q: a friend says: "if Rama's the perfect man, this scene means Hinduism says treat your wife like that." what fits today's teaching?
o: yes, that's exactly what it teaches.
many teachers read it as a king's duty, many Hindus side with Sita, and the tradition argues it openly.
Hindus aren't allowed to talk about this scene.
games.why: dharma is subtle: the scene is read as raja dharma, as a test, or as plainly wrong, and the argument itself is part of the tradition.

practice: Hindus have long argued over their stories out loud: in families, in satsang, in the commentaries. Today, try it. Think of one part of this story, or of your own tradition, that troubles you.
Breathe slowly, and say the question plainly, aloud or on paper, without rushing to an answer. If you pray, bring it to God as it is; the tradition lets Sita speak, and you can too.
If you don't, simply hold the question with respect. Asking honestly is part of the practice.

wordCard.voice: The fire. It begins with Rama's cold words to Sita in front of everyone, a moment Hindus still argue over.

orig.note: Sanskrit rājadharma: the duty of a king, from rājan, king, and dharma, duty or right order.

carryVoice: Your line: raja dharma, and the freedom to question it. Sita has not spoken yet. Rest gently tonight.
